back: The eye-tracking reading pattern on text-heavy pages: horizontal scans across the top, then down the left edge, like the letter F. Put key content in the top-left and upper areas.
Reading pattern on simple hero pages: across the top, diagonal, across the bottom (like Z). Good for landing pages with a headline and a call to action in the bottom-right.
Arranging page elements by importance using size, colour, spacing and position so users notice the most important content first.
A fictional but realistic profile of a typical user (age, goals, habits, frustrations) used to design content and features for real people.
An element that prompts the user to act — e.g. 'Buy now', 'Join free', 'Contact us'. Usually a button or link placed prominently.
A small feedback animation triggered by user action (button press, like button). Uses of motion should always have a purpose, not just decoration.
A navigation bar that stays visible while the user scrolls, so navigation is always one click away.
A navigation icon (three stacked lines) that expands a menu — commonly used on mobile to save space.
A navigation trail showing where the user is (e.g. Home > Music > 1970s). Improves orientation and accessibility.
Ensuring the site displays and works consistently across different browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge) and devices.
Search Engine Optimisation — techniques like keywords, descriptive titles, meta descriptions, alt text and fast mobile-friendly pages that improve search engine ranking.
A site that customises the experience or controls access to content, usually powered by a server and database (e.g. member areas, recommendations).
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, published by the W3C — the international standard for making web content accessible (contrast, keyboard navigation, captions, etc.).
A diagram showing the structure of the website — every page and how they link together. Required evidence for the assignment.
A low-fidelity layout of a page showing structure and element placement (boxes, placeholders) — no colour or final styling. One per page for the assignment.
A high-fidelity representation of the page showing colours, images, typography and branding — how the page will actually look.
The consistent look of the site: colour palette, branding, typography choices applied across all pages.
Creating, sourcing, preparing and organising assets: writing copy, editing images, compressing, naming files consistently and logging sources.
A table tracking each asset — name, source (original work or where downloaded, with credit) and where it is used on the site.
Reviewing designs to check quality (clarity, detail), user experience and whether they meet the client's requirements — then improving them.
Using meaningful tags (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <footer>) that describe structure — improves accessibility and SEO.
Every element is a box: content → padding → border → margin. Understanding it is essential for layout and spacing.
A CSS rule (@media) that applies styles based on viewport size — the basis of responsive design.
Collapsible sections that expand and contract (powered by JavaScript) — ideal for FAQs and long content lists.
An overlay dialog on top of the page — commonly used for image lightboxes and sign-in forms.
Alternative text describing an image for screen readers, shown if the image fails to load. Required for accessibility.
Testing that the site works: links, buttons, forms, interactivity and responsiveness. Recorded in a test plan (expected vs actual outcome).
Getting real users (classmates, friends) to try the site and give feedback on navigation, clarity, accessibility and experience.
Reflecting on the finished site: quality vs similar sites, suitability for audience/purpose, meeting client requirements, consistency and readability — then refining.
Legal protection for created work (images, text, music, video). Using others' work without permission breaches the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
Data protection law covering personal data collected by websites — privacy policy, consent, only collecting what you need, safe form handling.
Placing related elements together (grouping) and using white space/lines to separate different content — improves scanability.
